claim: L5 corticofugal neurons project to the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate body.
source: We first injected canine adenovirus 2 (CAV2-Cre) into the inferior colliculus, which selectively infects local axon terminals to express retrogradely in upstream projection neurons (N = 6 mice, Figure 1A: left) (Soudais et al., 2001; Schneider et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016). We then made a second injection of a Cre-dependent virus in the ipsilateral ACtx to label the corticotectal axon fields as well as other potential downstream targets (Figure 1A: left). As expected, we observed a smattering of smaller neurons in L6b that project to the midbrain, but a majority of cells in L5b with prominent apical dendrites (Figure 1A: left) (Schofield, 2009). In addition to dense terminal labeling in the external and dorsal cortex of the IC (Figure 1C: left), we also observed axon terminals in the MGBd (Figure 1B: left), as well as in the striatum and lateral amygdala (data not shown, see Asokan et al., 2018).
evidence: Anatomical tracing experiments using retrograde viral labeling from the inferior colliculus combined with anterograde labeling from auditory cortex showed terminal labeling in both IC and MGBd.

claim: L5 CF neurons deposit giant axon terminal collaterals in the dorsal division of the medial geniculate body (MGBd).
source: L5 CF neurons deposit giant axon terminal collaterals in the dorsal division of the medial geniculate body (MGBd, (Ojima, 1994; Bajo et al., 1995; Rouiller and Welker, 2000)), en route to additional downstream targets in the tectum, striatum, and amygdala (Deschênes et al., 1986; Bourassa and Deschênes, 1995; Bourassa et al., 1995; Rockland, 1998; Veinante et al., 2000; Kita and Kita, 2012; Asokan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: L6 CT projections are restricted to the thalamus.
source: L6 CT projections are restricted to the thalamus, with axon collaterals that densely innervate GABAergic neurons in the thalamic reticular nucleus en route to the ventral subdivision of the MGB (MGBv, (Lund et al., 1979; Staiger et al., 1996; Zhang and Jones, 2004; Llano and Sherman, 2008; Guo et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2018; Chevée et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: L6 CT axons densely innervate GABAergic neurons in the thalamic reticular nucleus.
source: L6 CT projections are restricted to the thalamus, with axon collaterals that densely innervate GABAergic neurons in the thalamic reticular nucleus en route to the ventral subdivision of the MGB (MGBv, (Lund et al., 1979; Staiger et al., 1996; Zhang and Jones, 2004; Llano and Sherman, 2008; Guo et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2018; Chevée et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: L6 CT axons collateralize extensively within the local cortical column, predominantly synapsing onto neurons in layers 5a and 6.
source: Unlike L5 CF neurons, auditory L6 CT axons also collateralize extensively within the local cortical column, predominantly synapsing onto neurons in layers 5a and 6 (Prieto and Winer, 1999; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: 97% of Ntsr1-positive neurons in the auditory cortex are L6 CT neurons.
source: We used the Ntsr1-Cre transgenic mouse to label L6 CT neurons based on our prior report that 97% of Ntsr1-positive neurons in the ACtx are L6 CT, and 90% of all L6 CT neurons are Ntsr1-positive (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: 90% of all L6 CT neurons are Ntsr1-positive.
source: We used the Ntsr1-Cre transgenic mouse to label L6 CT neurons based on our prior report that 97% of Ntsr1-positive neurons in the ACtx are L6 CT, and 90% of all L6 CT neurons are Ntsr1-positive (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Ntsr1-Cre expressing cells do not project to the inferior colliculus.
source: Labelling was not observed in the ipsilateral IC (Figure 1C: right), indicating that the Ntsr1-Cre expressing cells are separate from other classes of L6 projection neurons that have more distributed local and sub-cortical targets (Briggs, 2010; Sundberg and Granseth, 2018).
evidence: Anatomical tracing showed no labeling in the IC when Ntsr1-Cre mice were used.

claim: Few phototagged L5 CF neurons (4.5%) had spike shapes in the fast-spiking range.
source: Few of our phototagged neurons had spike shapes in the FS range (L5 CF: 4.5%, L6 CT: 9.6%), suggesting that these projection neurons are largely separate from the sub-population of parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic projection neurons (Rock et al., 2018; Zurita et al., 2018).
evidence: Quantification of spike waveform characteristics from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Few phototagged L6 CT neurons (9.6%) had spike shapes in the fast-spiking range.
source: Few of our phototagged neurons had spike shapes in the FS range (L5 CF: 4.5%, L6 CT: 9.6%), suggesting that these projection neurons are largely separate from the sub-population of parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic projection neurons (Rock et al., 2018; Zurita et al., 2018).
evidence: Quantification of spike waveform characteristics from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: L5 CF neurons are largely separate from the sub-population of parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic projection neurons.
source: Few of our phototagged neurons had spike shapes in the FS range (L5 CF: 4.5%, L6 CT: 9.6%), suggesting that these projection neurons are largely separate from the sub-population of parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic projection neurons (Rock et al., 2018; Zurita et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on the low percentage of fast-spiking neurons among phototagged cells, combined with citations to studies on parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic projection neurons.

claim: L5 CF units tend to have bursting spike patterns during sensory stimulation.
source: We confirmed that L5 CF units tended to have bursting spike patterns during sensory stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F), as suggested from current injections into L5 neurons recorded in acute slice preparations (Connors et al., 1982; McCormick et al., 1985; Agmon and Connors, 1992; Joshi et al., 2015).
evidence: Analysis of interspike interval distributions from electrophysiological recordings, supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: L5 CF neurons are more broadly tuned than L6 CT neurons.
source: While there were no overall differences in tuning bandwidth between neurons in L5 and 6, L5 CF neurons were more broadly tuned than L6 CT neurons (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, p=0.03, Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical comparison of frequency response area bandwidths measured from pure tone responses.

claim: Neurons in L5, including L5 CFs, exhibited tone-evoked first-spike latencies that were approximately twice as long as L6.
source: Neurons in L5, including L5 CFs, exhibited tone-evoked first-spike latencies that were approximately twice as long as L6 (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; layer: p<2×10−9, cell-type: p<4×10−4, Figure 3D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of tone-evoked first-spike latencies measured from pure tone responses.

claim: Responses in L6 were sparser than L5.
source: Responses in L6 were sparser than L5 (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, p<3×10−3, Figure 3G) and complex sound selectivity was sparser in L6 CTs than L5 CFs, in agreement with the differences in pure tone tuning bandwidth (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, p=0.02, Figure 3G).
evidence: Statistical comparison of sparsity indices calculated from responses to spectrotemporally modulated noise bursts.

claim: Complex sound selectivity was sparser in L6 CTs than L5 CFs.
source: Responses in L6 were sparser than L5 (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, p<3×10−3, Figure 3G) and complex sound selectivity was sparser in L6 CTs than L5 CFs, in agreement with the differences in pure tone tuning bandwidth (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, p=0.02, Figure 3G).
evidence: Statistical comparison of sparsity indices calculated from responses to spectrotemporally modulated noise bursts.

claim: Tuning bandwidth and sparsity were inversely correlated.
source: Tuning bandwidth and sparsity were inversely correlated (Pearson's r = −0.3, p<2×10−8, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but we found no other significant correlations between other tuning parameters (sparsity vs latency: Pearson's r = 0.06, p=0.27, bandwidth vs latency: Pearson's r = 0.08, p=0.07, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Correlation analysis of tuning parameters measured from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Classification of neuron type based on tuning parameters was better than classification based on cortical layer.
source: Classification was better than chance (50%) in either case, although classification errors were significantly lower based on projection cell-type than for cortical layer (32% vs 23%, p<0.05, Figure 4C).
evidence: Support vector machine classification analysis of tuning parameters.

claim: Variance in sensory response properties can be better predicted by classification of neuron type, rather than just cortical layer.
source: This indicates that variance in sensory response properties can be better predicted by classification of neuron type, rather than just cortical layer.
evidence: Inference from the SVM classification results showing lower misclassification rates for cell-type than layer.

claim: The CGF model outperformed the linear STRF model on 93% of cells.
source: The CGF model outperformed the linear STRF model on 93% of cells (Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, L5: p<2×10−52, L6: p<5×10−44, L5 CF: p<2×10−12, L6CT: p<3×10−7, Figure 5B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of predictive powers from two different computational models fit to neural responses to dynamic random chord stimuli.

claim: Optogenetic activation of L5 CF axons elicited weak, brief polysynaptic activation of deep layer RS and FS units.
source: Optogenetic activation of L5 CF axons with a 1 ms laser pulse elicited weak, brief polysynaptic activation of deep layer RS and FS units (Figure 6A: left).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings during optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Photoactivating the thalamic terminals of L6 CT units drove powerful, sustained, and distributed activation of local FS and RS units.
source: By contrast, photoactivating the thalamic terminals of L6 CT units drove powerful, sustained, and distributed activation of local FS and RS units (Figure 6A: right).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings during optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: L5 CF evoked spiking rapidly extinguished in nearby RS and FS neurons.
source: Whereas L5 CF evoked spiking rapidly extinguished in nearby RS and FS neurons, a single pulse of light to L6 CT axon terminals drove a volley of polysynaptic activity lasting approximately 20 ms in local RS and FS cells (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; L5 CF→FS (n = 96) vs L6 CT→FS (n = 63): p<4×10−4, L5 CF→RS (n = 501) vs L6 CT→RS (n = 296): p<3×10−25, Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Statistical comparison of normalized firing rates during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: A single pulse of light to L6 CT axon terminals drove a volley of polysynaptic activity lasting approximately 20 ms in local RS and FS cells.
source: Whereas L5 CF evoked spiking rapidly extinguished in nearby RS and FS neurons, a single pulse of light to L6 CT axon terminals drove a volley of polysynaptic activity lasting approximately 20 ms in local RS and FS cells (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; L5 CF→FS (n = 96) vs L6 CT→FS (n = 63): p<4×10−4, L5 CF→RS (n = 501) vs L6 CT→RS (n = 296): p<3×10−25, Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Statistical comparison of normalized firing rates during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The peak firing rates in L5 CF and L6 CT neurons during optogenetic activation were similar.
source: Differences in the magnitude and timing of feedforward activation were not reflected in the degree of direct activation of the L5 CF and L6 CT themselves, as the peak firing rates in both cell-types were similar (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; p=0.64, Figure 6D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of peak firing rates during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Functional coupling between L6 CT neurons and RS neurons was stronger than between L5 CF neurons and RS neurons.
source: The cross-covariance between RS neurons and both subtypes of sub-cortical projection neurons were relatively weak, although this interaction was stronger for L6 CT neurons (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; L5 CF↔RS (n = 2353) vs L6 CT↔RS (n = 981): p<5×10−8, Figure 7D–E).
evidence: Statistical comparison of cross-covariance integrals calculated from spike train correlations during sensory stimulation.

claim: Functional coupling with FS GABAergic interneurons was stronger overall and was particularly pronounced in L6 CT units.
source: Functional coupling with FS GABAergic interneurons, by contrast, was stronger overall and was particularly pronounced in L6 CT units (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; L5 CF↔FS (n = 448) vs L6 CT↔FS (n = 209): p<5×10−4, Figure 7D–E).
evidence: Statistical comparison of cross-covariance integrals calculated from spike train correlations during sensory stimulation.

claim: 65% of the L6 CT and FS pairs were lead-preferring.
source: The percentage of lead-preferring interactions were similar across L5 CF and RS/FS pairs, and L6 CT and RS pairs, at approximately 48%. By contrast, 65% of the L6 CT and FS pairs were lead-preferring, underscoring the biased directional interaction between L6 CT neurons and neighboring FS GABAergic neurons.
evidence: Quantification of the temporal peak of cross-covariance functions.

claim: L6 CT spikes tend to lead FS spikes, while the reverse is true for L5 CF spikes.
source: We observed that L6 CT spikes tend to lead FS spikes, while the reverse is true for L5 CF spikes (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; L5 CF↔FS (n = 56) vs L6 CT↔FS (n = 54), p<8×10−4, Figure 7H).
evidence: Statistical comparison of lead-lag asymmetry indices calculated from cross-covariance functions.

claim: L6 CT neurons can dynamically regulate the gain of deep layer ACtx networks by driving networks of deep layer FS interneurons.
source: These results echo previous reports that L6 CT neurons can dynamically regulate the gain of deep layer ACtx networks by driving networks of deep layer FS interneurons (Bortone et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from the current study's functional connectivity results, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L5 CF neurons are canonical broadcast neurons that integrate sensory inputs for transmission to distributed downstream targets.
source: Our findings underscore a duality among sub-cortical projection neurons, where L5 CF units are canonical broadcast neurons that integrate sensory inputs for transmission to distributed downstream targets, while L6 CT neurons are positioned to regulate thalamocortical response gain and selectivity.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity patterns.

claim: L6 CT neurons are positioned to regulate thalamocortical response gain and selectivity.
source: Our findings underscore a duality among sub-cortical projection neurons, where L5 CF units are canonical broadcast neurons that integrate sensory inputs for transmission to distributed downstream targets, while L6 CT neurons are positioned to regulate thalamocortical response gain and selectivity.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity patterns.

claim: L5 CF neurons exhibit broader stimulus selectivity with sluggish response latencies and extended temporal non-linearities.
source: Whereas L5 CF neurons showed broad stimulus selectivity with sluggish response latencies and extended temporal non-linearities, L6 CTs exhibited sparse selectivity and rapid temporal processing.
evidence: Summary of sensory characterization results from the study.

claim: L6 CT neurons exhibited sparse selectivity and rapid temporal processing.
source: Whereas L5 CF neurons showed broad stimulus selectivity with sluggish response latencies and extended temporal non-linearities, L6 CTs exhibited sparse selectivity and rapid temporal processing.
evidence: Summary of sensory characterization results from the study.

claim: L5 CF spikes lagged behind neighboring units.
source: L5 CF spikes lagged behind neighboring units and imposed weak feedforward excitation within the local column.
evidence: Summary of functional connectivity results from the study.

claim: L5 CF neurons imposed weak feedforward excitation within the local column.
source: L5 CF spikes lagged behind neighboring units and imposed weak feedforward excitation within the local column.
evidence: Summary of functional connectivity results from the study.

claim: L6 CT spikes drove robust and sustained activity, particularly in local fast-spiking interneurons.
source: By contrast, L6 CT spikes drove robust and sustained activity, particularly in local fast-spiking interneurons.
evidence: Summary of functional connectivity results from the study.

claim: Corticofugal neurons broadly fall into two classes: intratelencephalic and sub-cortical.
source: Corticofugal (CF) neurons broadly fall into two classes: intratelencephalic and sub-cortical (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intratelencephalic projection neurons in the auditory cortex are often found in layer 5a.
source: In the auditory cortex (ACtx), intratelencephalic projection neurons are often found in layer (L) 5a, project locally to L2/3, and distally to ipsi-and contralateral cortex and striatum (Games and Winer, 1988; Winer and Prieto, 2001; Yuan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ACtx sub-cortical projection neurons are found in L5b and L6.
source: By contrast, ACtx sub-cortical projection neurons are found in L5b and L6 and target auditory processing centers in the brainstem, midbrain, and thalamus, in addition to telencephalic targets outside of the central auditory pathway, including the striatum and lateral amygdala (Winer, 2006; Bajo and King, 2012; Asokan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The largest compartment of the auditory CF projection system comes from neurons in layer 5 and 6 of the cortex that innervate the medial geniculate body.
source: The largest compartment of the auditory CF projection system comes from neurons in layer 5 and 6 of the cortex that innervate the medial geniculate body (MGB) (Ojima, 1994; Prieto and Winer, 1999; Winer et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L5 CF neurons are regarded as the canonical 'broadcast' neurons of the cortex, pooling inputs from the upper layers and transmitting signals to widespread downstream targets.
source: L5 CF neurons, with their elaborate dendritic processes and far-ranging axons are regarded as the canonical 'broadcast' neurons of the cortex, pooling inputs from the upper layers and transmitting signals to widespread downstream targets (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Slater et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L6 CT neurons appear specialized for thalamocortical gain control.
source: L6 CT neurons, by contrast, appear specialized for thalamocortical gain control given that their axons terminate in all three nodes of the thalamo-cortico-thalamic loop: the MGB, GABAergic cells in the thalamic reticular nucleus and intrinsically, within the local column (Olsen et al., 2012; Bortone et al., 2014; Crandall et al., 2015; Crandall et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on anatomical connectivity patterns, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Differences between L5 CF and L6 CT neurons have been described in their cell morphology, intrinsic membrane properties, and synaptic properties.
source: Differences between L5 CF and L6 CT neurons are not limited to anatomical projections, as additional dichotomies have been described in their cell morphology, intrinsic membrane properties, and synaptic properties (Diamond et al., 1969; Andersen et al., 1980; Ojima, 1994; Bajo et al., 1995; Bartlett et al., 2000; Rouiller and Welker, 2000; Llano and Sherman, 2009; Sherman and Guillery, 2011; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L5 CF neurons utilize dense, non-linear coding of sound features.
source: We show that L5 CF neurons utilize dense, non-linear coding of sound features and have little influence on intra-columnar processing whereas L6 CT neurons have sparse selectivity for sound features, and strongly modulate local processing within ACtx.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity.

claim: L5 CF neurons have little influence on intra-columnar processing.
source: We show that L5 CF neurons utilize dense, non-linear coding of sound features and have little influence on intra-columnar processing whereas L6 CT neurons have sparse selectivity for sound features, and strongly modulate local processing within ACtx.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity.

claim: L6 CT neurons have sparse selectivity for sound features.
source: We show that L5 CF neurons utilize dense, non-linear coding of sound features and have little influence on intra-columnar processing whereas L6 CT neurons have sparse selectivity for sound features, and strongly modulate local processing within ACtx.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity.

claim: L6 CT neurons strongly modulate local processing within ACtx.
source: We show that L5 CF neurons utilize dense, non-linear coding of sound features and have little influence on intra-columnar processing whereas L6 CT neurons have sparse selectivity for sound features, and strongly modulate local processing within ACtx.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity.

claim: Each class of sub-cortical projection neuron performs distinct operations on incoming sensory signals.
source: These findings indicate that each class of sub-cortical projection neuron performs distinct operations on incoming sensory signals, which likely impart distinct effects on their downstream targets.
evidence: Inference from the study's findings on sensory processing and connectivity differences.

claim: L5 CF and L6 CT neurons likely impart distinct effects on their downstream targets.
source: These findings indicate that each class of sub-cortical projection neuron performs distinct operations on incoming sensory signals, which likely impart distinct effects on their downstream targets.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed differences in sensory processing and connectivity.

claim: CAV2-Cre selectively infects local axon terminals to express retrogradely in upstream projection neurons.
source: We first injected canine adenovirus 2 (CAV2-Cre) into the inferior colliculus, which selectively infects local axon terminals to express retrogradely in upstream projection neurons (N = 6 mice, Figure 1A: left) (Soudais et al., 2001; Schneider et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CAV2-Cre properties.

claim: NBQX blocks glutamatergic transmission within ACtx.
source: To verify this, we blocked glutamatergic transmission within ACtx with local application of NBQX, an AMPA receptor antagonist, in a subset of anesthetized control mice (N = 4, n = 188, Figure 2E).
evidence: NBQX is a known AMPA receptor antagonist, which is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: NBQX did not affect the low-jitter mode of antidromic spike latency distribution but eliminated spikes with variable first-spike latencies.
source: NBQX did not affect the low-jitter mode of the distribution but eliminated spikes with variable first-spike latencies, confirming that the low-jitter mode of the distribution reflected direct activation of the recorded projection neuron, whereas higher jitter spikes arose through local polysynaptic activation (Figure 2E: top).
evidence: Experimental results from pharmacology control experiments.

claim: Low-jitter antidromic spikes reflect direct activation of the recorded projection neuron.
source: NBQX did not affect the low-jitter mode of the distribution but eliminated spikes with variable first-spike latencies, confirming that the low-jitter mode of the distribution reflected direct activation of the recorded projection neuron, whereas higher jitter spikes arose through local polysynaptic activation (Figure 2E: top).
evidence: Inference from the NBQX pharmacology experiment results.

claim: Higher jitter antidromic spikes arose through local polysynaptic activation.
source: NBQX did not affect the low-jitter mode of the distribution but eliminated spikes with variable first-spike latencies, confirming that the low-jitter mode of the distribution reflected direct activation of the recorded projection neuron, whereas higher jitter spikes arose through local polysynaptic activation (Figure 2E: top).
evidence: Inference from the NBQX pharmacology experiment results.

claim: Broadly tuned sensory receptive fields in L5 CF neurons could reflect a more extensive convergence of intracortical inputs on their elaborate dendritic fields.
source: Broadly tuned sensory receptive fields could reflect a more extensive convergence of intracortical inputs on their elaborate dendritic fields, more broadly tuned excitatory thalamocortical input and narrower inhibitory input received di-synaptically through local fast-spiking interneurons (Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; Hooks et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculation about mechanisms underlying broad tuning, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most L5 CF neurons fall into the class of L5 pyramidal neurons referred to as intrinsic bursting (IB).
source: Most L5 CF neurons fall into the class of L5 pyramidal neurons referred to as intrinsic bursting (IB), based on their tendency to fire bursts of action potentials in response to depolarizing current injection (Connors et al., 1982; McCormick et al., 1985; Llano and Sherman, 2008; Joshi et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on bursting patterns observed in the current study, supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: In vivo whole cell recordings from physiologically identified IB neurons revealed broader frequency tuning than neighboring cell-types.
source: In vivo whole cell recordings from physiologically identified IB neurons revealed broader frequency tuning than neighboring cell-types, consistent with our observations of increased frequency tuning bandwidth in bursting L5 CF neurons (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: L6 CT cells are more densely interconnected with long-range inputs from sensory, retrosplenial, and cingulate cortices compared with neighboring corticocortical L6 neurons.
source: Compared with neighboring corticocortical L6 neurons, L6 CT cells are more densely interconnected with long-range inputs from sensory, retrosplenial, and cingulate cortices (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018; DeNardo et al., 2015), providing a potential source for multisensory response properties (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Long-range inputs from sensory, retrosplenial, and cingulate cortices provide a potential source for multisensory response properties in L6 CT neurons.
source: Compared with neighboring corticocortical L6 neurons, L6 CT cells are more densely interconnected with long-range inputs from sensory, retrosplenial, and cingulate cortices (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018; DeNardo et al., 2015), providing a potential source for multisensory response properties (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation about the functional implications of anatomical connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: The sparse tuning of L6 CT neurons is likely shaped by strong interactions with the local inhibitory surround, or the temporal relationship between excitation and inhibition.
source: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons in L6 are innervated by thalamocortical axons, suggesting that the sparse tuning of our L6 CT population is likely shaped by strong interactions with the local inhibitory surround, or the temporal relationship between excitation and inhibition (Zhou et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation about mechanisms underlying sparse tuning, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L6 CT neurons receive more input from local inhibitory neurons than L5 projection neurons.
source: This is consistent with recent anatomical work in barrel cortex, showing that L6 CT neurons receive more input from local inhibitory neurons than L5 projection neurons (DeNardo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous anatomical study.

claim: Highly selective, sparse sensory tuning has been described in L6 CT neurons in primary visual cortex.
source: Highly selective, sparse sensory tuning has also been described in L6 CT neurons in primary visual cortex, underscoring that the differences described here likely reflect an organizational motif shared across brain areas (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study in visual cortex.

claim: The differences in L5 CF and L6 CT neurons likely reflect an organizational motif shared across brain areas.
source: Highly selective, sparse sensory tuning has also been described in L6 CT neurons in primary visual cortex, underscoring that the differences described here likely reflect an organizational motif shared across brain areas (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference from the similarity of findings across auditory and visual cortex.

claim: L6 CT neurons propagate information that is sparse and more selective.
source: The L6 CT neurons propagate information that is sparse and more selective, but their anatomy places them in a position to modulate information both en route to the thalamus (through the TRN), but also locally through local networks of GABAergic FS interneurons.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings on sensory processing and anatomical connectivity.

claim: L6 CT neurons are positioned to modulate information both en route to the thalamus (through the TRN) and locally through local networks of GABAergic FS interneurons.
source: The L6 CT neurons propagate information that is sparse and more selective, but their anatomy places them in a position to modulate information both en route to the thalamus (through the TRN), but also locally through local networks of GABAergic FS interneurons.
evidence: Inference from anatomical connectivity patterns and functional connectivity results.

claim: L6 CT circuits may provide a behaviorally-relevant gating mechanism that can act on thalamic inputs to ACtx.
source: Indeed, previous work has suggested that these circuits may provide a behaviorally-relevant gating mechanism that can act on thalamic inputs to ACtx (Yu et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L6 CT circuits allow for rapid modulation of response gain.
source: Such circuitry also allows for rapid modulation of response gain and has led to speculation that L6 CT circuits play a crucial role in dynamically regulating stimulus salience according to internal state variables such as anticipation and attention (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011; Buran et al., 2014; Carcea et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from circuit properties, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L6 CT circuits play a crucial role in dynamically regulating stimulus salience according to internal state variables such as anticipation and attention.
source: Such circuitry also allows for rapid modulation of response gain and has led to speculation that L6 CT circuits play a crucial role in dynamically regulating stimulus salience according to internal state variables such as anticipation and attention (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011; Buran et al., 2014; Carcea et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation about functional roles, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L5 CF neurons integrate input from multiple ACtx layers.
source: Thanks in part to their elaborate dendritic structure, L5 CF neurons are able to integrate input from multiple ACtx layers and broadcast a dense, non-linear signal to multiple sub-cortical auditory stations.
evidence: Inference from anatomical structure and functional properties observed in the study.

claim: L5 CF neurons broadcast a dense, non-linear signal to multiple sub-cortical auditory stations.
source: Thanks in part to their elaborate dendritic structure, L5 CF neurons are able to integrate input from multiple ACtx layers and broadcast a dense, non-linear signal to multiple sub-cortical auditory stations.
evidence: Summary of the study's findings on sensory processing and anatomical connectivity.

claim: CF neurons have been implicated in guiding sub-cortical reorganization of behaviorally relevant sounds.
source: CF neurons have been implicated in guiding sub-cortical reorganization of behaviorally relevant sounds (Gao and Suga, 1998), enabling experience-dependent learning (Bajo et al., 2010), and gating innate defense behaviors (Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CF neurons have been implicated in enabling experience-dependent learning.
source: CF neurons have been implicated in guiding sub-cortical reorganization of behaviorally relevant sounds (Gao and Suga, 1998), enabling experience-dependent learning (Bajo et al., 2010), and gating innate defense behaviors (Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CF neurons have been implicated in gating innate defense behaviors.
source: CF neurons have been implicated in guiding sub-cortical reorganization of behaviorally relevant sounds (Gao and Suga, 1998), enabling experience-dependent learning (Bajo et al., 2010), and gating innate defense behaviors (Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ascending sensory pathways are classically characterized as two streams: a lemniscal system for higher fidelity propagation of detailed stimulus information and a non-lemniscal system that captures contextual sensory influences and internal state variables.
source: Ascending sensory pathways are classically characterized as two streams: a lemniscal system for higher fidelity propagation of detailed stimulus information and a non-lemniscal system that captures contextual sensory influences and internal state variables (Hu, 2003; Lee, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: A division of labor between two parallel, complementary streams is maintained in the corticofugal pathway.
source: Here we show that a division of labor between two parallel, complementary streams is maintained in the corticofugal pathway, highlighting a unifying theme in the organization of central sensory pathways.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study's findings in the context of broader sensory pathway organization.
